Alchemists spent two thousand years trying to make gold and failed, and we took the wrong lesson from it.

The lesson we took: gold is scarce.

The lesson actually available: nobody had worked out how yet.
On 21 October 2026, Marathon Fusion said it produced stable gold from mercury using fusion neutrons — about 10× what CERN recorded in 2025. The demo was reportedly in September.

The physics isn't exotic. Fast neutrons from deuterium–tritium fusion hit mercury-198. It becomes mercury-197. That decays to gold-197 — ordinary, stable, indistinguishable gold.

The mercury sits in the reactor blanket, where the reaction also breeds its own tritium.

Now the caveats, which are load-bearing and most coverage skipped them:

The company published gamma-ray spectra but NO mass, NO purity figure and NO cost.

The spectra don't establish how much, how pure, or whether it scales. Not independently verified.

Scale check, because the headline and the reality are orders of magnitude apart.

CERN's ALICE made ~29 PICOGRAMS of gold across four years of LHC running.

10× a picogram-scale result is still a picogram-scale result.

The tonnage everyone quoted comes from elsewhere: a 2025 paper MODELLING ~2 tonnes of gold per gigawatt-thermal per year.

The flashier “5,000 kg/yr” restates it per gigawatt ELECTRIC. Different denominator — that's how a modelled 2 becomes a marketed 5.

And Marathon's current reactor? About one kilowatt of fusion power.

A millionth of a gigawatt.

Against that: global gold mine supply was ~3,672 tonnes in 2025 (World Gold Council). USGS says nearer 3,300 — a methodology gap worth knowing rather than averaging away.

A gigawatt plant at the modelled rate adds under 0.1% of annual supply.

So: the gold price is not under threat from this. Anyone saying otherwise is ahead of the data.

What changed isn't the supply. It's the category.

Here's the part worth sitting with.

~212,000 tonnes of gold have ever been mined. NOBODY PROMISED THAT.

There's no protocol, no issuer, no document committing the universe to that number.

Gold's scarcity is an OBSERVATION about how hard it's been to get more.

Every observation of that kind is a statement about current cost — not about permanence.

The constraint was never a law forbidding it. It was an energy bill nobody could pay. Energy bills move.

The honest description of gold isn't “scarce forever.”

It's: scarce as long as making it costs more than buying it.

That's real, it's held for all of recorded history, and it's probably good a while yet. It's just a different claim than people think they're making.

Which brings us to blockspace.

It's also scarce — for an entirely different reason. Not because making more is expensive, but because A RULE SAYS HOW MUCH THERE IS.

Published in advance. Enforced by every node. Checkable by anyone.

You don't have to trust an assay, a vault or a mint. You don't have to believe anyone's cost estimate.

The supply is a number in a spec that thousands of independent machines agree on — and if it changed, you could see it change.

Now the honest counterweight, because stopping there would be a sales pitch.

A rule is only as durable as the people who can change it. Parameters get changed. Chains fork. Governance votes pass. “Enforced by consensus” means consensus can decide otherwise.

So rule-based scarcity isn't stronger in some absolute sense. It's DIFFERENTLY fragile.

A cost curve erodes quietly over decades and you learn about it from a press release — which is roughly what just happened to gold.

A parameter change happens in public.

Call it a gold rush if you like, but notice what's being claimed.

In a real gold rush the resource was physically there and whoever dug first got it. The claim was a hole in the ground.

Now the claim is a rule everyone can read.

For the whole history of money, the hardest part of a scarce asset was PROVING the scarcity. Assays, vaults, audits, trusted mints — and a long tail of people who turned out to be lying about what was in the basement.

Scarcity you can verify yourself, without trusting whoever's telling you about it, is new.

Newer than crypto prices. And it'll matter longer.

None of which makes anything a good investment, and we're not telling you to buy anything.

The useful question about whatever you hold: what enforces its scarcity — physics, cost, a rule, or a promise?
